questionStem: A32-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-week history of mild headaches and fatigue. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He does not smoke cigarettes. He drinks two to three beers nightly. Four months ago, he began a highly stressful new job, in which he has a verbally abusive boss. He says he has financial concerns and is worried about job security. He used to exercise three times weekly but stopped exercising 3 months ago because he is “too busy.” He lives alone and is not in a romantic relationship. He appears tired and withdrawn and responds to questions with short phrases. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.A: Addition of a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug to the medication regimen
choices.E: Placement in a nursing care facility

correctExplanation: Frailty is commonly encountered in older patients as a result of a variety of factors and presents with multiple problems across medical, functional, and social domains. In this scenario, this older patient who lives alone presents with several medical comorbidities that have resulted in difficulty performing activities of daily living. A multidisciplinary geriatrics assessment involves an evaluation by a team of several different specialists and may include physicians, occupational or physical therapists, social workers, and home health nurses or aids. A multidisciplinary assessment can help to identify the patient's needs and goals and address medical, physical, and social challenges while coordinating an overall plan to meet these goals and to regularly assess progress. The patient in this scenario may benefit from pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic treatment of her osteoarthritis, physical therapy to improve mobility, assessment by a home health nurse to improve her ability to function independently, as well as a social work assessment to ensure that she has adequate social support.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Addition of a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug to the medication regimen (Choice A) is an appropriate option for the treatment of this patient's osteoarthritis but is less likely to address all of her functional difficulties with activities of daily living. A multidisciplinary geriatrics assessment can help to identify her needs prior to planning for pharmacologic therapy. Intra-articular administration of a corticosteroid (Choice B) is an appropriate choice for treatment of osteoarthritis, particularly of the knee or hip, that is refractory to more conservative treatment with exercise and topical or oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. This patient's osteoarthritis affects a variety of joints and has led to multiple problems with activities of daily living, including opening pill bottles and cooking. Injection of corticosteroids alone is both premature at this time and also unlikely to address all of her functional difficulties with activities of daily living. Orthopaedic consultation (Choice D) is not necessary at this time. Osteoarthritis is best managed initially with conservative treatment including exercise and topical or oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Refractory pain involving certain joints can be treated with intra-articular corticosteroid injections. correctExplanation: The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends various screening tests and interventions for patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus should be screened for high blood pressure at every medical visit. Lipid profile screening should be done at least every 5 years to measure total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and triglycerides. An annual urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio test and blood test to measure serum creatinine should be performed to detect early-stage kidney damage. Comprehensive eye examination, foot examination, depression screening, weight management counseling, and tobacco cessation counseling are also recommended annually. However, guidelines may need to be individualized based on a patient's specific clinical characteristics and comorbidities. Given that this patient has had all the above studies except for a foot examination at the visit 3 months prior, this is the most appropriate step at this time.

questionStem: A64-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 1-year history of a nonhealing lesion on her left lower leg. She reports that the lesion does not itch, bleed, or drain. She has not attempted any treatments or remedies, and she does not wear any clothing or other items that rub the affected area. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination of the left lower extremity discloses the findings shown in the photograph. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This patient has a presentation consistent with acute epididymitis, and the most appropriate next step in management is antibiotic therapy. Acute epididymitis, or infection of the epididymis, most commonly presents with unilateral scrotal pain associated with a tender, swollen mass over the posterior aspect of the testis. In severe cases, such as this patient's, it can also present with localized erythema, dysuria, and systemic symptoms such as fever and rigors. Physical examination will show an intact cremasteric reflex, which helps differentiate acute epididymitis from testicular torsion, in which the cremasteric reflex is often absent. The underlying cause is most commonly infection with Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae in men under age 35 years, whereas Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas species are the more common causative organisms in older men or in men having unprotected insertive anal intercourse. Evaluation should include urine nucleic acid amplification testing for both C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae, as well as urinalysis and urine culture. Treatment includes empiric ceftriaxone to cover gonorrheal infection and doxycycline or azithromycin to cover chlamydial infection in patients at risk for sexually transmitted infections. Levofloxacin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are the recommended agents for patients at low risk for sexually transmitted infections. Symptomatic management includes scrotal elevation, application of ice, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Scrotal elevation and warm baths (Choice B) are not the most appropriate next step in management. While scrotal elevation can aid in symptomatic management of acute epididymitis, warm baths would likely worsen the erythema and edema associated with it. Rather, ice should be used to treat the associated symptoms. Additionally, failure to treat acute epididymitis with antibiotic therapy could lead to worsening of the infection with abscess formation or spread of the infection to surrounding structures (eg, testes). Ultrasonography of the scrotum (Choice C) may be used to aid in diagnosis of acute epididymitis. Doppler ultrasonography of the affected testes would show increased blood flow to the inflamed epididymis. However, acute epididymitis is most commonly diagnosed clinically. Delaying treatment with antibiotics to pursue further imaging would increase the likelihood of complications associated with the infection. If the leading diagnosis were testicular torsion, ultrasonography would be the next step, along with emergent urological consultation. Referral to a urologist (Choice D) on an emergency basis would be appropriate for the management of testicular torsion, which is caused by the rotation of the testes around the spermatic cord with consequent ischemia and necrosis. questionStem: Item 1 of 2 | Which of the following screening tests is most appropriate at this time?

choices.D: Test of the stool for occult blood

correctExplanation: Osteoporosis is a metabolic bone disease characterized by diffusely low bone density. Evaluation for osteoporosis involves a DEXA scan and is defined as a bone mineral density less than 2.5 standard deviations compared to a young, normal population (T-score). The United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends, at the Grade B level, to screen women over age 65 years for osteoporosis, and under age 65 years when increased risk factors exist. The most common risk factors for the development of osteoporosis are age, smoking, chronic inflammatory disease, corticosteroid use, and estrogen-depleting conditions in women. Osteoporosis is often asymptomatic but increases the risk for fractures, most commonly involving the hip, vertebrae, and distal radius. Calcium and vitamin D supplementations are recommended for treatment and prevention of osteoporosis. Recommendation should be made for weight-bearing exercise in the absence of other contraindications to slow deterioration of bone mineral density. Bisphosphonates inhibit osteoclast activity and can be used to treat osteoporosis to reduce further loss of bone mineral density. For this 66-year-old patient, a DEXA scan is the most appropriate screening test at this time.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Acellular pertussis (Choice A) vaccine protects against pertussis. Pertussis occurs as a result of an infection from Bordetella pertussis and may lead to severe paroxysmal coughing, which may be accompanied by cyanosis and followed by syncope, emesis, or apnea. Acellular pertussis vaccine is typically administered along with tetanus and diphtheria vaccines. Vaccination against pertussis provides a good degree of protection for the first several years following vaccination, but this protection commonly wanes over time. Booster vaccinations are recommended every 10 years. Cirrhosis does not confer an increased risk for pertussis. Haemophilus influenzae type b, conjugated (Choice B) vaccine is not indicated for this patient. H. influenzae is a gram-negative bacterium that can result in various mucosal infections, such as conjunctivitis, otitis media, bronchitis, and pneumonia. Asplenic patients are at risk for infection with encapsulated bacteria, and vaccination against encapsulated bacteria such as H. influenzae is indicated. Cirrhosis does not confer additional risk for infection with H. influenzae. Live Salmonella typhi (Choice C) vaccine provides protection against typhoid fever caused by S. typhi infection, which presents with fever, abdominal pain, rash, and diarrhea. Live S. typhi vaccine is recommended for travelers to areas where typhoid fever is endemic, such as South Asia, Africa, the Middle East, or South America. Live S. typhi vaccine is available as an oral live attenuated vaccine or an intramuscular conjugate vaccine. Patients with cirrhosis do not require routine vaccination against typhoid fever. Meningococcal vaccine (Choice D) protects against infection by Neisseria meningitidis, which may lead to life-threatening meningitis or sepsis. Meningococcal vaccine is available as a conjugate vaccine and a recombinant protein serogroup B vaccine. The conjugate vaccine is indicated for all children and is administered in two doses, the first between ages 11 and 12 years and the second at age 16 years. The serogroup B vaccine is given as an additional dose, usually between ages 16 and 18 years. Certain adult patients at particular risk for meningococcal disease, such as patients with HIV infection or men who have sex with men, benefit from an additional dose of meningococcal vaccine every 2 to 3 years throughout life. Cirrhosis does not confer additional risk for meningococcal disease. Educational Objective: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices recommends routine vaccination for protection against pneumococcal disease for infants, children, and adults age 65 years or older. It is recommended that the patient in this scenario receive the pneumococcal 23-valent polysaccharide (PPV23) vaccine at this time because of his history of cirrhosis, which increases his risk for developing pneumococcal disease. Adults over age 65 years who do not have an immunocompromising condition (including cirrhosis), cerebrospinal fluid leak, or cochlear implant should receive one dose of the PPSV23 vaccine. Any patients who received the PPSV23 vaccine prior to turning age 65 years should receive a single additional dose after age 65 year and at least 5 years after the prior dose. 4 C e G 6 Score Report Lab Values Calculator

questionStem: A 22-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of thick, flaky fingernails. During this time, he also has had dry, scaly, red patches of skin on his forearms and chest. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. During the past 2 years, he has worked as a restaurant dishwasher. A photograph of the left hand and right forearm is shown; similar findings are seen over the left forearm and trunk. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin condition, often localized to sites of trauma, including the elbows and knees. Psoriasis is associated with production of tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-a, interleukin (IL)-12, IL-17, and IL-23 produced by keratinocytes, dendritic cells, and T-cells. The Th7 lymphocyte is thought to be central to the pathophysiology of psoriasis, and newer biologic therapies target the cytokines r released by these cells. questionStem: A37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of frequent headaches. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her last health maintenance examination 3 years ago showed no abnormalities. There is no family history of serious illness. She 45 |b); BMI is 24 kg/m2. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is ‘e 16/min, and blood pres: ion shows no abnormalities except for an epigastric bruit. Arteriography shows fibri tery. The underlying mechanism of this patient's condition was most likely initiated by the release of which of the following substances?
correctExplanation: Renal artery stenosis is a cause of secondary hypertension related to activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Low afferent blood flow to the affected kidney leads to abnormal stimulation of the juxtaglomerular apparatus and excessive production of renin. Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin |, which is then converted to angiotensin II by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) in the pulmonary vasculature. Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor that directly mediates systemic hypertension. Angiotensin I! also leads to increased Na* reabsorption in the renal tubules, aldosterone release by the adrenal cortex with subsequent increased Na” and fluid retention and hypokalemia, vasopressin release from the posterior pituitary leading to increased fluid retention, enhanced adrenergic function through inhibition of norepinephrine reuptake in sympathetic nerve endings, and stimulation of hypothalamic thirst centers. In younger patients, fibromuscular dysplasia is the most common cause of renal artery stenosis, while in older patients it is typically caused by atherosclerosis. An abdominal bruit may be disclosed in the region of the stenosis. Renal vein sampling may detect an increased renin concentration on the affected side. Diagnosis is established with renal artery doppler ultrasonography or MR angiography, which are able to quantify the degree of renal artery stenosis and associated renal atrophy. Treatment involves angioplasty or stenting of the stenosed renal artery to improve flow. ACE inhibitors can be considered for unilateral stenosis but can lead to acute renal failure in the setting of bilateral renal artery stenosis.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Aldosterone (Choice A), angiotensin | (Choice B), angiotensin II (Choice C), and angiotensin III (Choice D) would all be increased in this patient. Their increase occurs secondary to the primary release of renin, which is the chief driver of hypertension in renal artery stenosis. Educational Objective: Renal artery stenosis is a cause of secondary hypertension caused by abnormal activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system leading to excessive production of renin. Diagnosis is established with renal artery doppler ultrasonography or MR angiography, which are able to quantify the degree of renal artery stenosis and associated renal atrophy. 4 Previous Score Report Values Calculator
